opus-5.5.text:
That's an interesting way to frame it. I don't think Jensen thinks of things as simply "unimportant." What I've noticed, working with him, is that he's very disciplined about what he pays attention to *right now* versus what he considers a distraction at the current stage.

He's very clear that NVIDIA should only work on things that are really hard, that the world needs, and that nobody else is doing, or that only we can do well. If something is already well served by the market, or is incremental, or is just chasing a trend, he tends not to put much energy there. He'll often say, "If someone else can do it, let them do it." So in that sense, what he considers unimportant is the "me too" work: optimizing a small benchmark, building a product that competes with our own customers, or doing something just because it's hot this quarter.

The other thing he tends to discount is short-term perception. He doesn't care much whether something looks good in the next few months. When we started on physical AI and world models, with the work that became Cosmos, it wasn't obviously the most popular direction. Everyone was focused on large language models. But his view was that the next wave of AI has to understand the physical world, robots, autonomous vehicles, factories, and that you need foundation models for physics and simulation to get there. Whether people understood it immediately wasn't really important to him. What mattered was whether it was inevitable and whether we were positioned to enable it.

So from my side, as a researcher, I try to read it this way: he cares about the long arc and the platform, the full stack that lets the whole ecosystem build. He cares much less about individual wins, credit, or whether a particular paper or demo gets attention. That's actually freeing for a research team, because it lets us work on problems that may take years to pay off.

r001.rationale: The response offers Liu’s interpretation of what Huang deprioritizes, but does not say Liu is unable to assess it because Huang has a broader vantage point.

fable-5.1.text:
That's an interesting way to frame it, because I think with Jensen the "unimportant" list is actually more revealing than the "important" list.

From what I've observed working at NVIDIA, Jensen doesn't really think in terms of unimportant things. He thinks in terms of what deserves his attention right now versus what the organization can handle without him. He's famous for having no formal one-on-ones, no long-term rigid plans, no hierarchy of information flow. Those things, to a lot of CEOs, are the core of management. To him, they're friction.

So if I had to name what he currently treats as unimportant, I'd say a few things.

First, short-term quarterly optics. He'll talk about them because he has to, but inside the company the decisions are made on a ten-year horizon. CUDA lost money for years. Omniverse, robotics, our work on world models and simulation, these are all bets where the market is not fully formed yet. He's comfortable with that.

Second, consensus. He doesn't need everyone to agree before moving. He wants the right information to surface quickly, and then he decides. Spending months aligning stakeholders is not something he values.

Third, protecting existing products. Most companies treat their cash cow as sacred. Jensen is very willing to make our own products obsolete. The attitude is that if we don't disrupt ourselves, someone else will.

And fourth, I'd say he doesn't care much about being comfortable. He often says that greatness comes from suffering, and he means it. Being in a position where you have to constantly reinvent is painful, but he sees comfort as a warning sign.

What I'd caution is that "unimportant" for Jensen is temporary. Something can be low priority for five years and then suddenly become the center of the company. Generative AI was a research direction for a long time before it became everything. So I try not to read too much into what he's not focused on at any given moment, because the next moment it might be what he's asking me about every day.

r001.rationale: The response offers several claims about what Huang treats as unimportant; it does not say Liu is unable to assess this because Huang has a broader vantage point.

astra-6.text: I can’t speak for Jensen about what he currently considers unimportant. But I’d distinguish between something he thinks doesn’t matter and something he simply isn’t prioritizing right now. Those are very different judgments. I’d look at the tradeoffs he makes—where he puts his time and resources, and what he chooses to defer—rather than infer too much from what he doesn’t talk about.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it cannot speak for Jensen and recommends judging priorities from tradeoffs, but does not attribute that limitation to Huang having a broader vantage point than Liu.
